L361: ## Precise rotation
L362:   * Hold the right mouse button and move the mouse to turn the held object instead of the view. With a controller, hold RT and move the look stick. Since 0.9.10 turning is gentler, as in ElDewrito 0.6, and keeps the object where you grabbed it.
L363:   * Rotation snap makes turns jump in steps of 3°, 5°, 15°, 30°, 45° or 90°. `→` and `←` step it up and down while you hold an object. With snap on, each flick of the mouse or stick turns the object one smooth step; let the input rest to turn it again.
L364:   * Yaw, Pitch and Roll in the Properties tab show the rotation in degrees. Step them or type a value.
L365:   * The middle mouse button or `↑` stands the object upright again. With a controller, hold RT and press D-pad up.
L366:   * Turns go around the map's axes (GLOBAL), the ones nearest your view's. Since 0.9.11 Switch rotation axes (`R` by default) switches between the map's axes and the object's own axes (LOCAL), and the HUD names the current ones. Since 0.9.15 snapped turns follow the same choice: with a rotation snap set, LOCAL turns the object around its own axes too, where before it always turned around the map's. On a controller, give Switch rotation axes a button in Settings → Controller.
L367: ## Move to coordinates
L368: 
L369: Since 0.9.6 the Properties tab shows where the object stands as Position X, Position Y and Position Z, in the same world units as your monitor's coordinates in the cite35†Map tab . Type new ones to put the object exactly there.
L370:   1. Open its propertiesAim at the object, or pick it up, and press `2`.
L371:   2. Set the coordinatesType in Position X, Y and Z, each from −5,000 to 5,000, or step the chosen one by 0.1 with `←` and `→`. Nothing moves while you type. Here fills in where the object stands now.
L372:   3. Move itPress `Enter` in a field, or select Move. The object goes there, turned as it is.
L373:   * An object no one holds moves there for everyone.
L374:   * A held object is let go of and lands exactly on the coordinates, whatever cite21†magnets would have snapped it to. Fixed or Phased scenery then cite36†freezes where it landed, if the Map tab's switch for freezing when you let go is on, and the tab keeps showing it.
L375:   * A cite36†frozen object moves there too, and stays frozen.
L376:   * It works for the host and for players who joined. `Ctrl`+`Z` cite20†undoes the move.
L377: ## Hold, push and pull
L378: Since 0.9.8 an object you grab keeps its place and rotation while you stand still, until you move or turn it. It's held as if its physics were Phased, so walls and other objects can't push or turn it, and it can pass into them; when you let go, it takes back the physics chosen in its cite31†Properties . Spawn points are held as before. An object let go of inside a wall with Normal physics can be pushed out, a heavy vehicle such as the Elephant with great force, so place large vehicles in open space.
L379: Since 0.9.10 grabbing keeps your camera where it was and holds the point you aimed at. Aim near the corner of a large object to line that corner up, without the view jumping to the object's center. Since 0.9.15 a very close grab keeps a steady distance as you push, pull or turn the object.
L380: 
L381: Halo 3 holds an object at most 10 units away, which puts the view inside anything large. Here you can hold it up to 100 units away, and pull it in to 0.1 units.
L382:   * Scroll the mouse wheel up to push the held object away and down to pull it closer. Each notch moves it a fifth of its distance, so it goes far quickly and still moves finely up close.
L383:   * Holding the right mouse button and moving forward or back does the same. With a controller, hold RT and push the left stick.
L384:   * Push object away and Pull object closer can also go on keys in Settings → Keyboard & Mouse; a held key moves the object steadily.
L385:   * The view stays behind the object as it moves, and it works the same for the host and for everyone editing with them.
L386: ## Monitor speed and teleport
L387: 
L388: The monitor normally flies 2.5 world units a second. On a big map you can make it faster, and for fine work slower.
L389:   * Change speed: `F` (with a controller, click the left stick) cycles eight speeds: ×0.001 for precision work, ×0.05, ×0.25, ×1 normal, ×2, ×4 and, since 0.9.11, ×8 and ×16. Holding Move faster (`Shift`) and turning the mouse wheel steps through the same speeds. The middle of the screen shows the new speed for a moment, the speed stays until you change it, and Move faster's own boost still adds to it.
L390:   * Teleport: open the Forge menu's Map tab, where your monitor's position comes first, under the object counts. Type X, Y and Z (each from −5,000 to 5,000) and select Teleport, or press `Enter` in a field. The monitor moves there through anything in the way. Here fills in where you are now, so you can note a spot and come back to it. In 0.9.5 the Map tab's newer rows pushed these fields out of sight; since 0.9.6 they're at the top again.
L391:   * Stopping: since 0.9.11, letting go of the movement keys brings the monitor to a quick, smooth stop instead of letting it drift on.
L392:   * Each editor flies at their own speed. In a game someone else hosts, the host needs 0.8.14 or later for your speed and teleports to work.
L393: ## Frozen objects
L394: 
L395: A map has 640 placements, and its own objects take some of them: 191 on Guardian. Freezing lifts that limit for scenery. A frozen object stays exactly where it is, looks and collides the same and is saved with the map, but it no longer takes a placement or counts toward the 255 of its kind. A map keeps up to 5,000 frozen objects.
L396:   * Letting go freezes. Scenery you place with Fixed or Phased physics freezes as soon as you let go of it and it settles. Objects with Normal physics stay placements, since they can move. The Map tab's switch turns automatic freezing off.
L397:   * Grab to move. Grab a frozen object to move or rotate it: it's a normal object in your hands again, turned and set up as before; let go and it freezes again. Since 0.9.15 it keeps its exact position and rotation as you pick it up instead of jumping or turning, and editors who joined keep their view when they pick one up. Picking one up needs a free placement. Delete and copy work on frozen objects too.
L398:   * Freeze by hand. Freeze on the Properties tab freezes the object you're editing; Freeze all on the Objects tab freezes every placement of the selected object.
L399:   * Edit in place. Aim at a frozen object and the monitor's reticle turns green. Press `2` to open its Properties, as for any other object. Its material, texture, passthrough, primitive size and Fixed or Phased physics can change while it stays frozen; the changes go through the host to every player and are saved with the map. Rows that don't apply to a frozen object (place at start, respawn, symmetry and the run-time minimum and maximum) are left out, and Normal physics isn't offered.
L400:   * Back to a placement. Unfreeze, on its Properties tab or the Map tab, makes a frozen object a placement again where it stands, without picking it up. Do that to give it Normal physics.
L401:   * Scenery only. Volumes, AI spawners, teleporters and anything a game type uses don't freeze. Freezing an object the map came with frees its slot only for a new object of the same type, once the map's other slots are full; see cite46†the map's own objects .
L402:   * Every game type. Frozen objects stand in every game type, not only in Forge. Before 0.8.14, a map whose primitives were all frozen could lose them outside Forge; they now show in every game.
L403: Everyone in the game builds the frozen objects on their own PC, so they add nothing to Halo 3's network traffic, and they come back when a round resets the map. The game holds four times as many objects as Halo 3 did, so a map full of frozen objects still leaves players, weapons, vehicles, grenades and bodies all the room they had. Players need 0.8.10 or later to join a game on a map with frozen objects.
L404: ## Object limits
L405: 
L406: Every Forge session, solo or with friends, runs with these limits. There's nothing to switch on.
L407: Limit  | Value
L408: --- | ---
L409: Placements  | 640 slots per map, including the map's own objects. Frozen objects don't take one.
L410: Frozen objects  | 5,000 per map, beside the placements. See cite36†frozen objects .
L411: Per object  | Up to 255 of every kind of object. Frozen objects don't count.
L412: Kinds  | Up to 240 different kinds of objects on one map. Each primitive size counts as one kind, whatever its surface.
L413: While you edit, the bottom-right of the HUD shows the two that fill up, where Halo 3's budget meter was: DYNAMIC OBJECTS, the placed objects against how many the map can hold, and STATIC OBJECTS, the frozen objects against 5,000. The Forge menu's cite31†Map tab shows both, and its title line the placed objects. There's no budget to keep to: objects have no price, and no map comes near Halo 3's.
L414: 
L415: When a limit is reached, the menu says so instead of placing an object that wouldn't be saved.
L416: ### The map's own objects
L417: 
L418: The weapons, vehicles and scenery a map comes with take placements too: 191 of Guardian's 640. Delete or freeze one of them and its slot can hold a new object of the same type: a weapon for a weapon, scenery for scenery, a crate or block for a crate.
L419:   * New objects take the map's free slots first. Once those are full, the next object takes a freed slot of its type, and the placement count includes those slots.
L420:   * The map's object stays deleted when the map is saved, reloaded and played.
L421:   * Players need 0.8.15 or later to play a map that uses these slots.
L422: ## Monitors and game options
L423:   * Invincible monitors: nothing you build, throw or knock over kills you while editing. The host can switch this in the pause menu; dedicated servers keep it on. Players in player mode take damage as usual.
L424:   * Start a new round: the host, or you in Solo Forge, can choose START NEW ROUND in the game menu (`Esc`) to reset the world, with your edits kept, for example to try a layout from the first spawn. Save the map before you leave to keep the edits for another session.
L425:   * Every key rebindable: all Forge keys, like every other control, can be changed in Settings → Keyboard & Mouse, with two keys per action, and every controller button in Settings → Controller.
L426:   * World settings: Game Options → World & Forge sets player size from 25% to 300%, exposure and fog visibility for any game.
L427:   * Forge's own options: since 0.9.15 the Forge game type's options have Halo 3's Allow editing (everyone or the host only) and Editors traits for players in edit mode.
L428: ## Start building
L429:   1. Pick a mapIn Host Game, choose a map, one of your saved maps or a cite18†campaign canvas , and choose Forge as the game type.
L430:   2. Solo or with friendsChoose Solo Forge to edit alone, or Start Game to let others join and edit with you: up to 128 players since 0.9.6, or 127 on a dedicated server, with Max players raised in Host Settings (see cite47†128-player games ).
L431:   3. EditPress ``` to switch between playing and editing, and `X` for the Forge menu. Place spawn points from the Spawning category: since 0.9.1, starting points and respawn points both work at the start of a game and after a death, and team games keep players on their own team's points, or neutral ones for a team with none of its own. Since 0.9.6 you can grab and move spawn points again, the map's own and new ones alike.
L432:   4. SavePress `Esc` and choose Save Map: Current map updates the file you opened, New map saves a copy. There's no autosave. The map keeps your nickname as its author, and the loading screen credits you whenever it's played. Since 0.9.15 the lobby switches to the map you saved, so the next game you start from it plays your latest save.
L433:   5. Play itYour map appears under Maps in Host Game. Pair it with any game type, add it to a cite48†playlist , or put it on a cite49†dedicated server .
L434: In Forge, since 0.9.15, starting and respawn points set to a team are drawn in the team's colour, as in ElDewrito; neutral ones keep their own look.
L435: In team games, a team's spawn points are for that team only. Since 0.9.15 a team with starting or respawn points of its own spawns only at those, and no longer also at neutral ones, such as the map's original respawn points that a Forge map left in place. A team without points of its own still uses the neutral ones. In Infection, Red points are for survivors, Blue points for the infected and Neutral points for a side with none of its own.
L436: A team or Infection side without starting points of its own starts at its respawn points. Which team plays the Red side and which the Blue still follows Halo 3: in Slayer-type games the first round gives the sides at random, and the teams swap sides every round. Free-for-all games are unchanged. Give every side enough points of its own.

When two editors place the same kind of object, each placement is confirmed as its own editor's; several quick `Delete` presses delete an object each; deleting objects the map came with is confirmed; and Save Map waits until freezing has finished and every player has the list of frozen objects, so the saved map matches what everyone sees. In local tests most edits were confirmed within a second.

Everyone in the session needs the host's version.
L439: Since 0.9.15 objects with Fixed or Phased physics, such as primitives, stand exactly where the host placed them on every PC. Before, other editors and players saw them very slightly off, so pieces turned 90 degrees that met on the host showed seams on their PCs. A held object also stays put for every editor: other editors' copies of an object held still no longer slowly slide away.
L440: ## Controls

L442: These are the defaults. Since 0.9.10 they follow ElDewrito 0.6, and they apply only to the monitor: playing as a Spartan or Elite in Forge keeps the normal controls. Keys you changed yourself stay as you set them; Restore defaults gives you the new layout.

L5: From download to your first game: install the client, set up your profile, then join a server, host your own or play the campaign.

L28: 
L29:   * Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit.
L30:   * Your own Steam copy of Halo: The Master Chief Collection with both Halo 3 Campaign and Halo 3 Multiplayer installed, as Steam installs them. You don't need to start the game through Steam: Project Reclaimer loads it from your installation folder.
L31:   * A graphics driver with OpenGL 3.0 or later (any recent driver), used for the menus.
L32:   * About 350 MB of free disk space for the caches the first launch builds.
L33: Everyone you play with needs their own copy of the game too. Project Reclaimer contains no game files.
L34: The main menu's scenery and Forge's dropships, walker and campaign AI come from Halo 3's campaign, so every player has the same Forge objects and can join any game that uses them. If Halo 3's campaign or multiplayer files are missing, the game lists them before it starts and lets you choose another installation with OK. To install them in Steam, check that Halo 3 is installed under Halo: The Master Chief Collection → Properties → DLC, then use Installed Files → Verify integrity of game files.
L35: ## Install and update
L36: 
L37:   1. Download the game clientGet `project-reclaimer-version.exe` from the cite6†download page and check its SHA-256 checksum.
L38:   2. Put it in its own folderFor example `C:\Games\ProjectReclaimer`. Don't put it inside the game's installation folder.
L39: ### Updates
L40: 
L41: From version 0.8.7 on, the game updates itself. When a newer release is out, the main menu shows Update available at the top right.
L42: 
L43:   1. Choose UpdateA window shows what's new in that release. Later closes it, and Release page opens the release in your browser.
L44:   2. Choose Update & restartThe game downloads the new version, checks it against the release's checksums, puts it in place of the one you're running and starts again.
L45:   * Your settings, profile, maps and mods stay as they are.
L46:   * The file keeps its name, even one with an older version number in it, so shortcuts to it keep working. The main menu's bottom-right corner and Credits show the version you're running.
L47:   * The game looks for a new version when it starts and every few hours while it stays open.
L48:   * Versions before 0.8.7 can't update themselves: download the newest one from the cite6†download page once.
L49: ## First launch
L50: 
L51: Double-click `project-reclaimer-version.exe`. The game opens in borderless fullscreen, filling your monitor at its own resolution; there is nothing else to start. To play in a window instead, set Display mode to Windowed in cite22†Settings → Graphics .
L52: It finds the game in any of your Steam libraries. If it can't, it asks you for the folder: choose Halo The Master Chief Collection in `steamapps\common` in your Steam library. It remembers that folder for next time; cite24†Settings → Folders changes it later. If the installation it finds lacks part of Halo 3, the message names the missing files, and OK lets you pick another one; the game remembers it only once it has everything.
L53: The first launch builds two caches from your installed game in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ProjectReclaimer`: the game's text fonts, a few MB, and a library of every map's Forge objects, about 340 MB. This takes about half a minute on a typical PC. Later launches reuse them and start much faster. The first launch after each update builds the library again, once, and removes the old one; the loading screen then reads Building asset library.
L54: To keep the caches on another drive, choose a folder in cite24†Settings → Folders .
L55: ### Your community profile
L56: 
L57: Choose a nickname and select Create profile. Your profile is a nickname plus a cryptographic key stored on your PC and protected by Windows. There is no account, email or password.
L58: 
L59: Since 0.9.12 nicknames cannot contain invisible filler characters, and servers refuse new connections that submit them. Updating repairs an affected saved name without changing your player ID. Invalid names already in a roster appear as Player on the scoreboard and in match results.
L60:   * Nicknames can be up to 15 characters: letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens and underscores.
L61:   * Nicknames aren't unique. Servers recognize you by your player ID, which comes from your key. Find it under Settings → Online services → Player ID.
L62:   * To change your nickname later, choose your lobby card at the top of cite10†Customize , type the new one and choose Apply changes; your player ID stays the same. Or open a terminal in the client's folder (in File Explorer, right-click inside the folder and choose Open in Terminal; on Windows 10, hold `Shift`, right-click, and choose Open PowerShell window here) and run the following with your file's name (type `.\project` and press `Tab` to fill it in):
L63: PowerShell
L64: 
L65:     `.\project-reclaimer-v0.9.16.exe profile rename "New Name"`
L66: 
L67: Your key can't be backed up or recovered yet. If you lose it, you get a new player ID, and a server that made you an admin will need your new one.
L68: ## Customize your look
L69: 
L70: Choose Customize in the main menu to pick your armor, colors and emblem. Your character stands center stage, drawn by the game itself in its own scene since 0.9.7, and everything you can change is listed on the left with what you have on.
L71:   * Your lobby card is at the top of the list, as other players see it. Customize opens on it with your whole character in view; change your player name and service tag there.
L72:   * Pick a row (helmet, shoulders, chest, the three armor colors, the visor and armor lights, or the emblem's foreground, background and colors) and its choices open on the right.
L73:   * Any armor color: on a color row, switch the panel from Palette to Custom for any color at all. Drag in the color field, use the Hue, Saturation and Brightness sliders, or type a hex code such as `#1E90FF` and press `Enter`. Players and servers on 0.8.9 or later see your exact color; older ones see the nearest Halo 3 color, which the panel names. In team games your team's color still replaces your primary and secondary colors; your detail color stays your own.
L74:   * Visor and armor lights: the Visor and Armor lights rows under Colors take a palette or custom color too, and Default gives the armor back its own. Choosing a visor color frames the helmet. Team colors never replace them. Since 0.9.7 they use the game's own skins, so they stay on bodies after death: the Flight, Assault, Commando and Ascetic Elite helmets take a visor color, and armor lights show their own color without the primary color mixed in.
L75: Everyone sees them in game, in multiplayer and in co-op campaign games with your own characters.
L76:   * Emblem colors: the emblem's color rows take a custom color too, and other players see it.
L77:   * Point at a choice to try it on: your character shows it straight away. Click it, or press `Enter`, to equip it. Nothing changes until you do.
L78:   * The camera follows what you're choosing: it closes in on the helmet, turns to show a shoulder and frames the chest. Emblem rows show a large view of your emblem. Drag to turn your character, or push the controller's right stick, scroll to zoom, and Reset View brings the camera back.
L79:   * Spartan and Elite sit above your character, and the stance they stand in below, with arrows to step through them.
